title: Low-frequency acoustic metamaterial absorption
bottleneck: Blocking low-frequency noise — traffic, aircraft, industrial hum — with thin structures is fundamentally hard because wavelengths are meters long while panels must be centimeters thick. Acoustic metamaterials with resonant inclusions can absorb narrow bands, but broadband low-frequency absorption in a thin, lightweight panel remains unsolved; resonances that work at 100 Hz fail at 150 Hz. Active cancellation helps but needs power and sensors everywhere.
why_it_blocks: Noise pollution is a major urban health burden linked to cardiovascular disease and sleep disruption. Without thin, passive low-frequency absorbers, buildings and vehicles must rely on mass — thick concrete and heavy insulation — which conflicts with lightweight, low-carbon construction.
current_state: Membrane-type and coiled-space metamaterials have demonstrated subwavelength absorption at targeted frequencies in the lab. Broadband, thin, and cheap panels that could be deployed in real buildings are still a research prototype, not a product.
